idiom_name: Dictionary<TKey, Func<...>> handler table + TryGetValue miss policy
implementation_notes: The BCL supplies both halves: `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` for the lookup and `Func<...>`/`Action<...>` delegates (or an interface) for the handlers, so the table is one entry per operation - `handlers.Add(Op.Add, (ctx, v) => ctx.Acc + v)` - and dispatch is `handlers.TryGetValue(op, out var h) ? h(ctx, arg) : throw new UnknownOpException(op)`. What replaces the classic structure is the dictionary plus first-class delegates: no class per command is needed while the handlers are stateless. When the discriminant is a closed enum or a sealed hierarchy, the C# 8+ switch expression (`op switch { Op.Add => add, Op.Sub => sub }`) is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler and is the better fit; keep the dictionary when the mapping is data-driven, large, or partly supplied at runtime through keyed DI or plugin registration.
pitfalls: `handlers[op]` throws KeyNotFoundException while `TryGetValue` merely returns false - choose one miss policy and apply it at the single dispatch site instead of mixing the two styles.
Delegate entries are closures: registering inside a loop without a per-iteration local captures the loop variable and every handler sees the final value.
A Dictionary is not safe for concurrent writers, so lazy self-registration from several threads races; freeze after startup (FrozenDictionary/ReadOnlyDictionary) or coordinate writes.
`Func<>`/`Action<>` entries are delegates rather than expression trees, so a table is not introspectable for route dumps or help text - keep a parallel metadata record if you need that.
